source.title: A Precise Performance Analysis of Learning with Random Features

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model complexity in random-feature models and reports generalization-error curves bearing on double descent, using a model class and method different from the deep-network settings in the claim.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the reported complexity-sweep generalization-error results in Figures 1 and 4. The paper also compares activations and losses in Figures 2 and 3, but those comparisons do not give condition-specific results on the fall-rise-fall curve. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: In random-feature models (two-layer nets with a fixed first layer), the paper derives exact asymptotic training and generalization errors and checks them against simulations. It reports fall-rise-fall generalization-error curves over model complexity η=k/m, with the peak where training error reaches zero. It also reports that strong regularization (λ=1) removes the peak. These are new-setting results on V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is an exact asymptotic characterization of training and generalization error for random-feature models with general activations, losses and feature matrices. This rests on the unproven uGEC. It rigorously confirms earlier replica predictions, and simulations show the generalization error follows a double-descent curve. The authors also say regularization, loss and activation help mitigate the peak, with λ=1 giving a monotone curve.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes random-feature models, equivalent to two-layer networks with fixed first-layer weights, and sweeps hidden-neuron model complexity. It does not reproduce the deep-network, epoch, or sample-size interventions in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve changes with regularization: λ = 1 gives monotone decreasing generalization error in Figure 4. The paper also describes mitigation effects associated with activation and loss choice.

fits_no_version.finding: Choice of activation (SoftPlus vs ReLU, Fig. 2) and loss (hinge vs LAD, Fig. 3) changes the height of the interpolation peak; LAD gives a higher peak than hinge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The height of the double-descent peak depends on the activation and loss function, beyond regularization strength.

fits_no_version.finding: The peak's location in η moves to smaller η as λ increases (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization shifts the location of the interpolation peak, not only its height.

record.problems: The paper bases its analysis on the uniform Gaussian equivalence conjecture, which it says remains to be rigorously proved. The numerical simulations are averaged over 50 trials, but no uncertainty estimates are stated. The prose does not separate the low-regularization Figure 4 curves by each λ value.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2 and 3 compare activation and loss choices and discuss mitigation, but the text does not report condition-specific fall-rise-fall results for those comparisons; no separate rows were extracted.

untested.parts: Only random-feature models with a fixed first layer; no deep networks.
No sweep over sample size near the interpolation threshold; α is fixed per figure.
No effective-complexity measure compared across axes. The peak is only tied to where training error hits zero, along the η axis.
The study does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether λ=1 is truly the optimal regularization.
No recounting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: LAD-loss classification (binary step activation, λ=10^-4, p=0.05 label flips) follows a double-descent curve with a higher peak than hinge loss.
Interpolation peak location decreases as λ increases.
SoftPlus activation lowers generalization error and reduces the interpolation peak relative to ReLU (regression, λ=10^-2).

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The theory depends on the uniform Gaussian equivalence conjecture, which is validated only by simulation. The curves are theory plus 50-trial Monte Carlo averages, with no error bars. The 'optimal regularization' claim rests on three λ values. I set the tranche to T3 rather than the record's T2, as a new model class and setting.

versions.untested_parts: The reported models are random-feature models with fixed first-layer weights, not tests of model-size double descent in deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported.
No sweep over the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold is reported.
The reported evidence is for random-feature models, not a survey of model classes generally.
The study does not compare effective complexity measures across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study varies regularization and reports a setting with monotone decreasing generalization error. It does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether the regularization setting is optimally tuned.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that changes the curve into an ordinary U shape.
